 A solar generator is a portable battery you can recharge with sunshine. The right one for you depends on whether you're powering a campsite or major home appliances.

 Why trust EnergySage? 
 EnergySage Solar isn't just for rooftops . A solar generator can keep your phone, laptop, and coffee maker running at a campsite, and the biggest models can now keep a refrigerator, a well pump, or a handful of home circuits running when the grid goes down.  
 The name is a bit misleading, though: A solar generator doesn't make electricity on its own. It's a battery-based portable power station that you can recharge with solar panels (or a wall outlet, or your car). That distinction matters when you're deciding how much to spend and what you can realistically expect it to power.  
 Below, we'll cover how solar generators work, our five picks for 2026, how to size one for your needs, and when a permanently installed home battery makes more sense. 
 Key takeaways
 Solar generators are portable battery storage systems powered by solar panels.  
 Unlike solar-plus-storage systems, solar generators are not designed to back up major appliances in an outage, though some can help.  
 You can compare solar generators by assessing the watts and watt-hours of the systems, as well as their battery chemistries.  
 The pros of solar generators include free renewable energy, low maintenance costs, and clean and quiet operation, while the cons include limited power supply, high upfront price, and slow charge time.  
 If you want backup power that's always connected to your home, consider a home battery instead.

 What are the best solar generators in 2026? 
 There's no single best solar generator, because what’s best for a weekend camper vs a homeowner with a well pump is going to be very different. We picked five solar generator models across a range of sizes and prices; each matched to a specific job.  
 1. EcoFlow Delta Pro 3: Best overall for home backup  
 EcoFlow's Delta Pro 3 is a strong pick for homeowners who want more than phone charging and a few lights. Its 120 and 240 volt (V) output can handle larger household appliances, like well pumps and electric dryers, and you can add batteries to reach 12 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of storage, which is roughly the same capacity as many of the top home batteries on the market today.  
 The trade-offs are price and size: at 113.5 pounds, it rolls on wheels rather than riding in your trunk. (Though if you don’t need 240 V output, EcoFlow's Delta 3 Ultra Plus offers over 3 kWh of storage and 3,600 W of output for $1,599, about half the price.)

 Our methodology 
 How we chose the best solar generators 
 We built this list from manufacturer specifications, current product availability, and recent independent research. EnergySage did not test these models for this update. We weighed six factors:  
 Storage and continuous output, since together they decide what you can run and for how long  
 Solar input, because faster solar charging matters most during multi-day outages  
 Battery chemistry and rated cycle life  
 Expandability and 240 V support for home-backup use  
 Weight and portability  
 Price, including what's actually in the box  
 We also chose models for different jobs instead of ranking five big batteries against each other. A 24-pound camping unit and a 137-pound home-backup station aren't competing for the same buyer.  
 What is a solar generator? 
 Put simply, a solar generator is a portable power station paired with solar panels. The power station holds a rechargeable battery, an inverter, and a bank of outlets and USB ports. The panels feed electricity to it during the day, so you can use that energy whenever you need it.  
 Some retailers use "solar generator" to mean the power station alone, while others save the term for a bundle that includes panels. Either way, the battery does the storing, and the panels do the generating. Most power stations also charge from a standard wall outlet or a car's 12-volt port, and some can recharge from a gas generator or an EV charger, so you aren't stuck waiting for a sunny day.  
 The key word is portable . A traditional home battery system is wired into your electrical panel by an electrician, but a solar generator works right out of the box. That makes it a good fit for camping, RV trips, tailgates, job sites, and keeping essentials running during an outage. The largest models blur the line a bit: Several of our picks can connect to a transfer switch or smart panel to run selected home circuits, which does require professional installation.  
 How do solar generators work? 
 A solar generator relies on four parts working together: solar panels, a charge controller, a battery, and an inverter. In today's all-in-one power stations, everything except the panels lives inside a single box.  
 Solar panels capture energy 
 When sunlight hits your panels, they produce direct current (DC) electricity. Portable solar panels are smaller and lighter than the panels you see on rooftops, and many fold up like a briefcase so you can reposition them to follow the sun. Many larger power stations also accept rigid, rooftop-style panels, as long as you stay within the unit's voltage and wattage limits.  
 A charge controller manages the flow 
 The charge controller sits between the panels and the battery and regulates incoming electricity, so the battery charges safely. Nearly every modern power station has one built in. The two main types are MPPT (maximum power point tracking) and PWM (pulse width modulation), and both are used in off-grid systems. MPPT controllers constantly adjust to pull more energy from your panels as sunlight and temperature change, which is why most current power stations use them. PWM controllers are simpler and cheaper, and you'll mostly find them in small DIY setups.  
 The battery stores the energy 
 Most new power stations use lithium iron phosphate (LFP, sometimes written LiFePO4) batteries. LFP batteries are typically rated for 3,000 charge cycles or more and are more thermally stable than older lithium chemistries. Some older and budget models still use nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) batteries, which are lighter but usually wear out sooner. Lead-acid batteries still show up in some DIY builds, but they're heavy and rare in today's portable power stations. Our guide to lithium-ion chemistries goes deeper on the differences.  
 An inverter converts energy for your devices 
 Batteries store DC electricity, but most household devices run on alternating current (AC). The inverter handles that conversion whenever you plug something into an AC outlet. Look for a pure sine wave inverter, which produces smooth, grid-quality power that's safe for laptops, medical devices, and appliances with motors. A pure sine wave inverter doesn't, on its own, let a power station connect to the grid; that takes compatible equipment and a proper installation.  
 Can you build your own solar generator?  
 You can. Van builders and cabin owners sometimes buy panels, a charge controller, a battery, and an inverter separately and wire them together. A DIY system lets you size each part exactly, but you're responsible for wiring, fusing, and making sure everything is compatible. For most people, an all-in-one power station is simpler and safer, and you can still choose your own panels as long as they fall within the power station's solar input specs.  
 How to choose the right solar generator 
 Start with what you want to power and work backward. Two numbers do most of the heavy lifting: watts and watt-hours.  
 Watts: How much it can run at once  
 Watts (W) measure power, or how fast a device uses electricity. A power station's continuous output rating tells you the most it can supply at one time. Add up the wattage of everything you plan to run together and make sure the total stays under that number. Appliances with motors, like refrigerators and pumps, briefly draw several times their running wattage when they start up, so check the surge rating too.  
 Watt-hours: How long it can run  
 Watt-hours (Wh) measure stored energy. In theory, a 1,000 Wh battery can supply 100 W for 10 hours, or 1,000 W for one hour. In practice, you'll get less. The inverter loses some energy converting DC to AC, and appliances don't draw a perfectly steady load. A conservative rule of thumb is to plan on about 80% to 85% of the rated capacity.  
 Take a refrigerator as an example. Check the yellow EnergyGuide label for its yearly energy use; 
 A fridge rated at 550 kWh per year uses about 1.5 kWh (1,500 Wh) per day.  
 Using the 85% rule, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh) could keep it cold for roughly 14 hours, while the EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus (3,072 Wh) could cover about a day and a half before it needs a recharge.  
 Five questions to ask before you buy a solar generator  
 What do you want to power? Phones and a laptop, a refrigerator and lights, or an energy-hungry appliance like a well pump? Your answer sets the minimum output and voltage you need.  
 How long do you need backup to last? A few hours of camping are very different from a two-day storm outage. Multiply your average load by the hours you need, then add a cushion for conversion losses.  
 How quickly can it be recharged? Compare maximum solar input and AC charging speed. Real-world solar charging depends on weather, season, panel angle, and how many panels you own. A unit rated for 2,400 W of solar input only charges that fast if you connect enough panels on a clear day.  
 Can you expand it later? Check which expansion batteries are compatible, what they cost, and whether adding capacity also adds output or 240 V support.  
 What's included in the price? Some listings cover the power station alone, while others bundle panels, cables, or home-backup accessories. Compare like with like. 
 Solar generators vs. gas generators: Pros and cons 
 Compared with a gas-powered portable generator, a solar generator trades unlimited refueling for clean, quiet, low-maintenance power.

 Pros of solar generators 
 Free energy from the sun 
 Once you own the panels, sunlight costs nothing, and the sun has never once raised its rates. You won't need to stockpile gas before a storm or make a fuel run after one.  
 Little to no maintenance 
 There's no engine, so there are no oil changes, spark plugs, or stale fuel to deal with. Beyond keeping the battery charged and the firmware updated, there's not much to do.  
 No exhaust, much less noise 
 Gas generators produce carbon monoxide and must run outdoors. The Consumer Product Safety Commission says more than 80 people die each year from carbon monoxide poisoning caused by portable generators, and it recommends running them at least 20 feet from your home. A solar generator produces no fumes, so you can use it inside. It's also far quieter than an engine, though cooling fans do kick on during fast charging or heavy loads. 
 Cons of solar generators  
 Limited by battery capacity 
 A power station can only deliver the energy it has stored. Small units are great for electronics, while large ones can run a fridge, sump pump, or well pump for hours or days. Either way, you'll need to manage what's plugged in during a long outage. Expandable models help, but extra batteries add cost.  
 Higher upfront cost 
 A solar generator usually costs more upfront than a gas generator with similar output, especially once you add panels. You'll make some of that back by skipping fuel and maintenance, but the upfront cost can feel daunting to some.  
 Recharging takes time 
 Unfortunately, you can't pour in a fresh tank of sunshine. Solar recharging depends on daylight and weather, and a cloudy week can slow you down. Many larger power stations— including the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3, Anker Solix F3800 Plus, and Bluetti Apex 300—can also recharge from a gas generator, which gives you a backup plan for long outages.  
 Solar generators vs. home batteries: Which is better for home backup? 
 A large power station can keep your essentials running, but it isn't a substitute for a permanently installed home solar battery. The right choice depends on how much of your home you want to power and how hands-on you want to be when the lights go out.

 Generator Buying Guide
 By 
 Allen St. John 
 Senior Home & Tech Writer 
 By 
 Yasmeen Khan 
 Home & Garden Writer 
 Lab testing by Paolo Fu , Scott Collomb and Jonathan Tuczynski 
 Updated October 1, 2026 
 During a power outage, a generator can keep all your necessities running—from the lights, appliances, and heating systems to your air conditioning , sump pumps , and WiFi. It can also help you save money by keeping your food from spoiling and your basement from flooding. For people with electrically powered medical devices, buying a generator can be a lifesaver.
 As more and longer power outages happen across the U.S., a generator is becoming an important layer of protection. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration , consumers experienced an average of 11 hours of electricity interruptions in 2024, nearly twice as many as a decade before. Major storms accounted for a vast majority of those outages. 
 While a generator can keep you afloat during severe weather, it can pose dangers if you don’t take precautions and set up your generator ahead of any storms. Working by flashlight (or in a rush), you might skip over critical safety steps while connecting a generator to appliances or the electrical panel in your home.
 To keep yourself safe, always use your generator outside, at least 20 feet from your home, with the exhaust directed away from the house. Before you fire it up, make sure your house has working carbon monoxide (CO) detectors , which can help prevent CO poisoning. And make sure to buy detectors that are UL 2034 certified or ETL listed, and be careful when purchasing detectors sold through third-party vendors like Walmart and Amazon. You’ll find good choices in our  ratings of CO detectors , which are free to anyone.
 CR also recommends having  low-level CO detectors , which are particularly important to protect older people, children, those with preexisting conditions, and pregnant women. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has more information on carbon monoxide poisoning and how to prevent it.
 Even if your generator has a built-in sensor that triggers an automatic shutoff if CO builds up to dangerous levels in an enclosed space, we advise you to follow the safety guidelines shown here.
 Illustration: Consumer Reports 
 Illustration: Consumer Reports 
 How Do I Calculate the Size of the Generator I Need?
 Choosing the right home generator means figuring out what size you need first . Generators are sold by power output, measured in watts. The amount of power a generator delivers determines how many electronics and appliances you can run at once. A typical home needs around 5,000 watts to run several major appliances and window air conditioners. But you’ll likely need more to power a whole heating/cooling system or high-demand heating appliances like electric dryers or ovens.
 Before you look through our generator ratings for the best generator for your home, make a list of the devices you’ll need when the power’s out. Then add up wattages to get you in the right ballpark. 
 Here are some rough wattage estimates for common essentials as you build out your list:
 Refrigerator : 300 to 800 watts
 Sump pump : 750 to 1,500 watts
 Space heater : 1,500 watts
 Window air conditioner : 1,000 watts
 Lights: 5 to 80 watts (per bulb)
 Computer : 60 to 300 watts
 Types of Generators
 When buying a generator, you have four options to consider: home standby generators, portable generators, inverter generators, and portable power stations.
 Home Standby Generators
 Home standby generators , or whole-house generators, are installed permanently on your property. They can run on natural gas or propane and kick in automatically during an outage.
 • They’re by far the most expensive and should be installed by an experienced electrician who can help with town or municipal permits, noise restrictions, and proper location. Installation usually costs more than the generator itself, sometimes several times more. 
 • Home standby generators start automatically when the power goes out, and they typically supply more power than the other three options.
 • Many units turn on automatically for a few minutes every day so that you know they’re ready to run when there’s an outage. They also run a self-diagnosis to let you know when maintenance is needed. Some even alert you or your dealer via email or text.
 • You have your choice of fuel—propane, which is less risky to store than the gasoline required for other models here, or natural gas, which provides an unlimited supply of power.
 • Whole-house generators, like portable generators, can pose a risk of carbon monoxide poisoning. Make sure to have working CO detectors in your home.
 Typical power output: 
Roughly 5,000 to 20,000 watts, but because there’s little difference in the installation costs between a smaller unit and a larger one, it makes sense to get one that can easily power your home both now and in the future.
 Typical cost: 
$3,500 to $7,000 without installation, which can more than double the cost.
 Home Standby Generators Ratings 
 Portable Generators
 Portable generators can be moved around. Some are smaller for transporting to a tailgate, while others are better kept on your property as a backup power source. 
 • These units tend to cost less than home standby generators, and there’s no installation expense unless you’re connecting one to your home’s electrical box.
 • Portable generators typically run on gasoline that you may need to store in large quantities. If you’re storing the unit for any length of time, you need to add a stabilizer to your gas to keep it from clogging the fuel system, which is why some units won’t start after sitting in a garage for months or longer.
 • A few models run on both gasoline and liquid propane. Running a generator on propane has the added benefit of being cleaner, so fuel residue doesn’t clog up your generator’s carburetor.
 • You can use portable generators anywhere on or off your property—but never in an enclosed space. Like a car engine, these models can quickly produce deadly levels of carbon monoxide. Always run a portable generator at least 20 feet from your house and equipment such as a central air conditioner condenser or a window AC, and direct the exhaust away from the house or any other structure, including your neighbors’ homes.
 • If it’s raining, shield your generator with a canopy designed for your particular model.
 • Some models offer electric starting. The battery required for electric start, however, might not be included.
 Typical power output: 
Models we test provide 3,000 to 8,500 watts.
 Typical cost: 
$400 to $2,000.
 Portable Generators Ratings 
 Inverter Generators
 Like portable generators, inverter generators can be moved around. They’re much quieter because they throttle up and down to match demand rather than running at full power all the time. They also have more sophisticated exhaust systems that help tamp down noise. But inverter generators generally cost more than portable generators with a comparable output. 
 • Inverter generators operate more efficiently, so you can get a much longer run time from the same amount of gasoline. They also produce fewer emissions than portable generators, but you should still follow the same safety precautions to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning.
 • Sizes vary widely, from large inverter generators that can power an entire house, generating 5,000 watts or more and exceeding 250 pounds, to small versions that can be taken on a camping trip, weighing as little as 30 pounds.
 Typical power output: 
Models we test provide 900 to 7,600 watts.
 Typical cost: 
$300 to $5,000.
 Inverter Generators Ratings 
 Portable Power Stations
 Portable power stations are large, rechargeable lithium-ion batteries that store electricity for when you need it. They have limitations, but they’re the only option for someone who lives in an apartment and can’t safely run a generator outdoors.
 • You charge it by plugging the unit into an electrical outlet or using an included solar panel (though it will charge very slowly via the panel).
 • As with a small inverter generator, a portable power station is best for shorter outages (hours, not days), and it can be great for a camping trip or tailgate. The units don’t provide as much power for as long as a portable generator and must be periodically recharged. Accompanying solar panels can help extend the battery’s run time. 
 • Because they have no engine, the devices are extremely quiet. They don’t produce fuel emissions or carbon monoxide, so you can use them indoors. And there are no problems with starting them because there’s nothing to start. Think of them as a giant version of the battery pack you use to charge your cell phone on the go. But they tend to be heavier and significantly more expensive than a comparably sized generator.
 Typical power output: 
Models we test provide 1,500 to 3,600 watts.
 Typical cost: 
$500 to $2500.
 Portable Power Stations Ratings 
 Generator Features to Consider
 Don’t let rain, snow, or wind keep you in the dark. Look for these options to get a generator that’s as safe as possible, reliable, and tailored to your power needs.
 Automatic CO Shutoff 
This critical safety feature automatically shuts down a generator’s engine if a built-in CO sensor detects that the deadly gas has reached certain levels. We have over a dozen generators in our ratings with a CO safety shutoff. (CR only recommends portable generators with this feature.)
 From Generac to Honda , more brands than ever offer options with this technology. You might see them advertised with marketing terms like “CO Guard” or “CO Protect.” But the only way to verify whether a generator meets one of the two standards is to look for one of these certifications on the packaging:
 • ANSI/UL2201 Certified for Carbon Monoxide Safety
• ANSI/PGMA G300 Certified Safety & Performance
 Low-CO Engine 
Brands including Ryobi and Echo are using a low-CO engine to guard against carbon monoxide poisoning.
 Automatic Start 
When the power goes off, the generator automatically starts without you lifting a finger. This is great if you travel a lot or work far from home and can’t always get there quickly in an emergency.
 Electric Start 
Several portable models offer electric start , a push-button alternative to the hassle of pull-starting the engine. If the battery isn’t included, make sure you factor in the added cost (around $50). Stationary models have automatic starting.
 Alternative Fuel Capacity 
Some portable generators come equipped to run on a propane tank or a natural gas line, and others can be converted with kits.
 Fuel Gauge 
You might appreciate being able to check a fuel gauge to see how much fuel is left in your portable generator, especially during blackouts.
 Low-Oil Shutoff 
If oil falls below minimum levels, the generator shuts down to prevent engine damage. While this feature is standard for stationary generators, it’s increasingly common on portables.
 Multiple Outlets 
Four or more outlets on a portable generator let you use its power more effectively by spreading the load, though we recommend using them for only a few devices at home or when you’re away—say, at a campsite. See the next section on transfer switches.
 Removable Console 
A removable console connects to the generator, allowing you to plug in appliances without running ( potentially risky ) extension cords outdoors.
 What’s a Transfer Switch and Do I Need One?
 A transfer switch is infinitely more convenient than an extension cord and allows you to safely connect a home standby or portable generator to your circuit panel with a single cable. You won’t need to worry about overloading extension cords, which could lead to overheating and fires.
 Using a transfer switch also means you can power essentials without a plug (overhead lights, well pumps, and water heaters, for example).
 Here are a few important notes on transfer switches:
 We recommend that you have a licensed electrician install your transfer switch. The average cost to install one is about $1,450, according to Angi . The electrician can also walk you through the process of turning your switch on and off.
 With whole-house generators , the transfer switch turns on and off automatically when the power shuts off or goes on, respectively. For portable models , you’ll need to flip a few switches by hand when the power goes out and switch them back to bring back grid power.
 Most transfer switches are designed for a 220-volt input, which means you’ll need a generator of 5,000 watts or more.
 You’ll need to choose which circuits are connected to the transfer switch. To do so, get a digital circuit breaker finder to determine which outlets and appliances are controlled by each circuit breaker in your panel. Then label them accordingly so an electrician can connect the circuits for all your essentials.
 If you’re looking to save money, you might be able to have an electrician install an interlock device instead. If it will work with your electrical system and meets local building codes, you’ll have to pay $50 to $150 for the interlock kit, plus $400 to $800 for labor, which is significantly less than you’d pay for a transfer switch. The kit allows your generator to power your home’s entire circuit breaker panel and prevents the generator from running once your electric service is restored. That’s important because running the generator after grid service is restored could fry your electronics and potentially shock a utility worker working near your home.
 A transfer switch is easier to use than an extension cord, allowing you to power entire circuits in your home more safely.
 Illustration: Chris Philpot 
 Illustration: Chris Philpot 
 How CR Tests Generators
 To test generator performance, our engineers load each model with various essentials you might want to power during an outage, like a space heater, well pump, or window air conditioner. We make sure the generator can handle the load it’s supposed to and also see what happens when a sudden spike in voltage hits, like if the compressor in your refrigerator kicks on when the generator is already close to capacity. The best models take that in stride, while others bog down or even quit. A high-output generator that struggles with power delivery or quality might stall or trip a circuit when it’s bogged down.
 We also consider how easy it is to move and use a generator, how efficiently it uses gasoline or other fuel, and how long it runs on a single tank.
 To test for safety, we run each generator through a variety of scenarios designed to capture the ways in which a consumer might inadvertently misuse it. Our custom-built test chamber is equipped with calibrated carbon monoxide (CO) sensors, and we record CO levels throughout the container while a generator is running, noting how quickly each generator shuts off when levels become potentially dangerous. 
 Finally, to reduce the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning, many portable generators feature a built-in sensor that triggers an automatic shutoff if CO builds up to dangerous levels in an enclosed space. CR only tests portable generators with this built-in sensor. Some generators also have engines that emit less CO to begin with. 
 Test data from CR shows that this safety feature is likely to save lives, and we’ll only recommend portable generators that pass our expanded CO safety technology test . 
 Generator Brands
 We test portable, inverter, home standby, and portable power station generators from brands like Briggs & Stratton and Ryobi in our labs.
 Briggs & Stratton 
 Briggs & Stratton makes portable , inverter , and home standby generators. In addition to manufacturing products sold under the Briggs & Stratton brand name, it makes gasoline engines used by other generator brands.
 Cat 
 Cat is a smaller manufacturer of gasoline-powered portable generators. It primarily focuses on the construction market, with generators designed for worksites.
 Champion 
 Champion is a smaller manufacturer of all kinds of generators, ranging from portable generators and small gas-powered inverter models to large standby generators that can power an entire house using propane or natural gas.
 DeWalt
 DeWalt is best known as a tool brand, but it makes gas-powered portable generators and inverter generators with contractors in mind. Its products are sold primarily at Home Depot.
 Echo
 Echo is a smaller outdoor power equipment company that’s new to the generator market. Most of its models are midsized; many of them have low-carbon-monoxide engines.
 Generac
 Generac is one of the largest generator manufacturers in the U.S. It makes everything from portable generators to home standby generators , and its products are widely available, including at Home Depot and through smaller dealers.
 Honda
 Honda has a reputation for making stellar generators, particularly inverter models. It sells its relatively expensive portable and inverter generators through small dealerships but not at home centers.
 Ryobi
 Ryobi is a tool brand exclusive to Home Depot. Its low-CO generator was the first on the market, and it offers inverter and portable models.

Best Portable Power Stations of 2026, LabTested and Reviewed - Consumer Reports 
 Skip to Main Content 
 Best Portable Power Stations of 2026, Lab-Tested and Reviewed
 We tested models from Anker, EcoFlow, and Goal Zero, among others, to find the ones that will provide power the longest and recharge quickly
 By 
 Allen St. John 
 Senior Home & Tech Writer 
 By 
 Yasmeen Khan 
 Home & Garden Writer 
 Lab testing by Paolo Fu 
 Updated September 2, 2026 
 When you shop through retailer links on our site, we may earn affiliate commissions.
 100% of the fees we collect are used to support our nonprofit mission.
 Learn more .
 A portable power station can quietly keep your devices running, but you have to pause every now and then to recharge the battery.
 Photo: EcoFlow
 If you’ve ever used a pocket-sized power bank to recharge your phone, you’ll appreciate the utility of a portable power station . It’s essentially a large rechargeable lithium-ion battery with an array of outlets you can use to power appliances and other devices in your home and on the road.
 It can keep your gear running at a campsite or a tailgate party and, yes, during a power outage, too (though only for a limited stretch of time). Keep in mind that portable power stations won’t keep electric appliances and devices running for nearly as long as comparably sized generators , says Paolo Fu, who leads generator and portable power station testing for Consumer Reports. But power stations can be a great alternative to generators during short outages, of say, a couple of hours, or may last longer if you’re powering only a few key essentials at once.
 “Portable power stations can be handy during an outage to charge your phone, make emergency calls, stay in touch with loved ones, and keep a fridge or freezer running a little longer,” Fu says. “They are best for outages that last for hours, not days.”
 In this article
 Best Portable Power Stations 
 What Can You Do With a Portable Power Station? 
 Portable Power Stations:
 Advantages 
 Disadvantages 
 Should You Buy a Portable Power Station? 
 How CR Tests Portable Power Stations 
 More on Generators & Emergency Power
 CR's Generator Ratings & Buying Guide 
 Best Portable Generators 
 Pros and Cons of Inverter Generators 
 Best Solar Panels 
 What to Eat During a Power Outage 
 Unlike a generator, a power station is sleek, quiet, and easy to use. It starts easily, without you having to worry about an engine that may have sat idle in the garage for months. It doesn’t saddle you with messy gasoline refills, clogged carburetors, or oil changes . Even more important, it eliminates the potentially deadly carbon monoxide fumes associated with generators.
 Before you rush out and buy one, though, consider the trade-offs. Power stations can be pricey and heavy, and the fastest way to recharge them is to plug them into an outlet, which is hard to do when the power’s out in your home. (You can slowly recharge them through their accompanying solar panels, and the solar panels can also extend the run time of your power station, but depending on the load, this may not be sufficient.)
 To help you weigh the pros and cons, we recently tested six popular models with their accompanying solar panels. They range in price from about $500 to more than $2,500. All have the capacity to provide backup power for key appliances in your home. They can also be quite large—ranging in size from a large car battery to a carry-on suitcase—and reasonably heavy, weighing 30 to nearly 100 pounds.
 For reviews of all the models we tested, check out our portable power station ratings and buying guide for more details.
 CR's Guide to Home Improvement
 Find  top-rated products and expert tips to help you save energy and money—and protect your home from extreme weather. 
 Best Portable Power Stations
 These are the best portable power stations from our tests, earning high marks for recharge speed, power delivery, power quality, portability, and ease of use. The prices (and our testing) include the power station plus its solar panels. The power stations can also be purchased separately, without the panels.
 What Can You Do With a Portable Power Station?
 The right-sized battery power station can deliver enough electricity to run essential systems and appliances, but only for a relatively short time. Smaller models can keep a laptop running and a few lights on, while much larger ones can be daisy-chained into a whole-house backup power solution.
 Your first task is to decide which devices and appliances you want to power and how much capacity you need to get the job done. Because a larger appliance like a refrigerator can kick on and off and cause a power surge, our experts recommend that you leave a little leeway between the total wattage of your appliances and the maximum power of your station. Energy Sage offers a guide on how much power appliances and other household electronics need.
 To help figure out what a portable power station can handle and for how long, take a look at the “claimed capacity” in watt hours (Wh) as well as the “claimed output” in watts in our ratings chart , Fu says. You’ll need to divide the power station’s capacity by its output to get a sense of how long the power station will run at full capacity.
 For example, the top model in our ratings, the EcoFlow Delta, has a claimed output of 3,600 watts and a claimed capacity of 3,600 watt-hours. If you want the EcoFlow working at full strength, delivering 3,600 watts to power all of the electronics you can—say, a refrigerator, laptop, television, five to 10 lights, and a medium window air conditioner—it would run for just one hour.
 If you want the EcoFlow to continuously power just your refrigerator, which draws about 700 watts, the power station would run for more than 5 hours on battery alone. (If you add the solar panel, it would extend the run time slightly, depending on solar conditions.) 
 A power station can also be used like an inverter generator to supply power at a campsite or a tailgate party. Indeed, power stations have become a staple on the road for those who revel in the adventures of van life . 
 They’re also a bit more flexible than generators at delivering power because they often supplement standard 120-volt, three-prong outlets with USB-A and USB-C ports for powering phones, laptops, and portable speakers.
 If you plan to take a portable power station on the road and use it outdoors, make sure you understand what kind of weather it can handle, Fu says. “Most solar panels we tested can handle any weather, but the power station itself may not be able to,” he says. “You don’t want to use the power station in the rain unless the manufacturer states that it’s waterproof.” 
 Or if you are using one in a dusty climate, make sure the manufacturer rates it for dust.
 Advantages of a Portable Power Station
 Here are the best reasons to invest in a portable power station:
 It’s quiet. Because it doesn’t have an engine, a portable power station is very quiet. Many don’t even have a cooling fan, so those—including the ones we’ve tested—are dead silent. (If your power station doesn’t have a cooling fan, Fu says to make sure to monitor it in the heat.) While tranquility may not be a huge consideration when your electricity is out, a near-silent power source at a campsite allows you to hear the lilting birdsong of a wood thrush instead of the rumble of a generator.
 It doesn’t emit dangerous carbon monoxide fumes. As a result, portable power stations don’t require the safety precautions of a generator, which include outdoor placement at least 20 feet from a home or garage, with the exhaust directed away from windows, doors, and air conditioners. You can run a power station in your kitchen, basement, or garage, so you don’t need an awning to keep the unit dry, as you would with a generator. That makes a power station a compelling alternative for apartment dwellers who want emergency backup power but lack the outdoor space to run a generator.
 It has excellent power quality. All of the power stations we’ve tested earn top marks for power quality, which is the ability to deliver clean power without the dips and spikes that can damage sensitive electronics. Their power quality is higher than most standard (noninverter) generators we’ve tested.
 Disadvantages of a Portable Power Station
 Here are the reasons you might choose to avoid a portable power station:
 It isn’t always convenient. The biggest disadvantage is that, like any battery, your power station will run out of power. And when that happens, you have to disconnect the unit and recharge it—a process that can take hours. That’s an inconvenience if you’re using the power station to charge your laptop, but it’s a major problem if you’re relying on it to keep food cold or power vital medical equipment. A generator has a big advantage here. Yes, it can run out of fuel, but when that happens, you just turn it off and refill the tank from a gas can, with only the briefest interruption of power.
 Its recharge rate can be slow. Not all portable power stations recharge at the same rate. When calculating Overall Scores, our testers assign the highest weight to recharge speed. Each of the models we’ve tested has portable solar panels that can recharge it, but the process is often slow, especially when the sky is overcast. You’re better off using the panels to extend the battery’s range, not to recharge it. And just as the power stations recharge at different rates, they deplete at different rates, too. Some are more efficient than others when powering the same load and can last longer.
 It’s heavy. And, for what it’s worth, portable power stations are not always easy to transport. Some heavier models come with wheels, like the 97-pound EcoFlow Delta Pro. But other models in our ratings don’t. CR evaluates handles as part of the portability rating because even lighter models—ranging from 30 to 60 pounds—should have one that’s easy to grip.
 It’s expensive. Finally, portable power stations are quite expensive. Our top-rated model—the EcoFlow Delta Pro—puts out 3,600 watts and costs more than $2,500. For comparison, you can buy a highly rated 3,900-watt inverter generator like the Generac iQ5200DF for about $1,000.
 Should You Buy a Portable Power Station?
 It ultimately comes down to how you plan to use it.
 Our ratings chart can help you zero in on a model that delivers high-quality power. But for many people, a gas-powered generator will be cheaper and more effective in a lengthy power outage, such as after a storm or other natural disaster.
 But if a portable power station’s most important virtues—quiet operation and the placement flexibility that comes with a lack of dangerous emissions—suit your needs, you might find it worthwhile to pay more than you would for a comparably sized generator.
 How CR Tests Portable Power Stations
 In our labs, CR test engineers evaluate five key measures to rate portable power stations: recharge speed, power delivery, power quality, portability, and ease of use. We don’t test the manufacturer’s run time claims, nor do we include noise evaluations in our ratings, because we found that, as a category, portable power stations run silently. 
 Recharge speed is based on how quickly the station charges while plugged into a 120-volt power source and while using the power station’s accompanying solar panels.
 Power delivery is based on how well the voltage is maintained and how well the unit handles surges in power. Higher power output means more equipment can be run simultaneously. Power quality reflects the station’s ability to deliver clean power over various loads. 
 To assess portability, we evaluate the power station’s ergonomics. To assess ease of use, we evaluate features including the number of outlets, USB port outputs, whether the power station has clear indicators of remaining power, and whether it comes with a companion app.
 Allen St. John
 Allen St. John has been a senior product editor at CR since 2016, focusing on digital privacy, audio devices, printers, and home products. He was a senior editor at Condé Nast and a contributing editor at publications including Road & Track and The Village Voice. He lives in Montclair, N.J., with his wife, their two children, and their dog, Rugby.

 Skip to Main Content 
 Portable vs. Whole-House Generator: Which Is Right for You?
 Both provide electricity during an outage—the choice comes down to convenience, price, and power
 By 
 Allen St. John 
 Senior Home & Tech Writer 
 Updated by Quentyn Kennemer Lab testing by Paolo Fu , Scott Collomb and Jonathan Tuczynski 
 Updated December 23, 2025 
 When you shop through retailer links on our site, we may earn affiliate commissions.
 100% of the fees we collect are used to support our nonprofit mission.
 Learn more .
 A portable generator (left) is much less expensive than a permanently installed whole-house model (right), but it's also more difficult to use and maintain.
 Photos: Emilie Harjes/Consumer Reports
 When the power goes out because of a hurricane, a storm, or a problem with the electrical grid, portable generators and whole-house generators will do the same important task: provide electricity until the power comes back on. But the two options are quite different in cost and convenience.
 Portable generators are generally stored in a garage, basement, or shed and wheeled into position outdoors when needed. Smaller models use extension cords to power a few small appliances, while larger portables connect to your electrical panel via a transfer switch to power hardwired appliances like well pumps and water heaters.
 Portable models tend to be noisier and produce less power than whole-house models, but they’re also much cheaper to buy and install than whole-house generators, which are installed permanently.
 In this article
 Pros and Cons:
 Whole-House Generators 
 Portable Generators 
 Safety Features on Portable Generators

 CR's Guide to a Winter-Ready Home 
 CR's Generator Ratings & Buying Guide 
 Best Portable Generators

 Why a Portable Generator Needs a Transfer Switch 
 The portable models in our generator ratings run on gasoline, burning through 12 to 20 gallons per day, depending on the unit’s output and the load being powered. That means you’ll have to store a significant quantity of gasoline, start the generator manually, and refill it (when it’s off, to minimize fire danger) after running it for several hours.
 An increasing number of models also run on liquid propane, the fuel many homeowners use for barbecue grills and other appliances. Of the 37 conventional generators in our ratings, 12 can work on both gas and propane. Among the 44 inverter models in our ratings, 12 can also run on propane.
 That gives you another fuel option when gas stations may not be operating at full capacity in the aftermath of a storm. Propane has the additional advantage of not clogging the fuel lines or the carburetor when the unit is in storage for a while.
 A whole-house generator, also called a standby or stationary generator, is permanently installed outside by a pro and has an insulated cover that helps to protect it from the weather and keeps it relatively quiet. It kicks on automatically when the lights go out and can power everything in your home at once. It can operate for days or even weeks on a full whole-house propane tank or indefinitely in the case of natural gas.
 “Home standby generators are expensive, but they’re the gold standard in backup power, and they outperform all other types of generators in our ratings,” says Paolo Fu, who leads generator testing at Consumer Reports. “If you can afford it, I’d tell you to pick a home standby generator every time.”
 But far more people choose portable generators for a simple reason: price. Here, we explain the pros and cons of each type of generator. Our buying guide offers deeper insights. CR members can read on for ratings and reviews of the top three models in each of the two categories. For more choices, browse our extensive generator ratings .
 Whole-House Generators
 Power output:  8,000 to 22,000 watts
 Price range:  $3,500 to $6,000
 Fuel needs:  13 to 48 gallons of liquid propane or natural gas per day
 Best for: If you face frequent outages that often last a long time and are willing to pay for the convenience of a generator that turns on automatically and runs almost indefinitely.
 Pros:   Whole-house generators are largely worry-free. They’re typically sized to power an entire house and turn on automatically. Propane models can run for days or weeks without refueling, while natural gas models can run indefinitely. They tend to be very quiet, and you don’t need to fuss with weather covers or canopies. 
 Cons:  Whole-house generators are pricier. And the installation costs can range from a few thousand dollars to $10,000 or more. That’s because you might need an electrician to hook up the generator to your electrical panel, plus subcontractors who can handle the plumbing for a gas or propane line and build a steady, permanent base for the generator. Models are also reasonably large—about as big as a central air unit—so you need to allocate space for one on the side or back of your house.
 Portable Generators
 Power output:  2,500 to 8,500 watts
 Price range:  $400 to $2,700
 Fuel needs: 12 to 20 gallons of gasoline per day
 Best for: If you’re on a budget, experience infrequent and relatively short power outages, and are willing to start the generator regularly to make sure it’s ready to go in an emergency.
 Pros:   Portable generators are much cheaper to buy and install. When a large portable model is connected to your home’s circuit breaker panel with a transfer switch it can power almost as much as a home standby generator. Both large and small units have built-in outlets to power appliances with suitable extension cords if you haven’t installed a transfer switch. Smaller inverter units can also be used for camping or tailgating.
 Cons:  You need to wheel your generator out of storage, connect it to your transfer switch, and fire it up each time there’s an outage. Portable models also require you to store large quantities of gasoline mixed with fuel stabilizer to get through a prolonged outage. They tend to be noisier and have a lower output than home standby models. 
 Safety Features on Portable Generators
 To reduce the risk of carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, new generators often feature a built-in sensor that triggers an automatic shutoff if CO builds up to dangerous levels in an enclosed space. Some models also have engines that emit less CO.
 All portable models in our ratings have one or both of these features, and we recommend portable generators only if they pass our CO safety technology test .
 But our findings also reveal hazardous gaps that automatic shutoffs fail to address, reinforcing why it’s critical to follow safety guidelines even if your generator is equipped with CO safety features.
 Never operate a generator indoors, including in an open garage, shed, or similar structure. 
 Position your portable generator at least 20 feet from your house with the exhaust directed away from it, as well as away from windows, doors, AC units, and other structures. 
 Make sure you’ve got a working battery-powered CO detector in your living spaces to warn you of a buildup of the colorless, odorless gas. 
 How to Run a Generator Safely
 Best Large-Capacity Portable Generators
 The largest portable generators in our ratings offer about as much power as the weakest whole-home generators at just a fraction of the unit and installation cost. Check below for more on the top three large-capacity models.
 Best Whole-House Generators
 Whole-home generators in CR’s ratings are separated by capacity. Large-capacity generators can provide 15,000 watts of power or more, while small-capacity models are those that deliver less than 15,000 watts for a considerably cheaper price. It is usually not worth buying if you only need emergency phone charging, expect a portable battery to run an entire home for days, rely heavily on electric heat or central air conditioning, or have no useful access to wall, vehicle, or solar recharging. 
The best way to decide is not to count features. Calculate how much energy you actually need each day, how much of that energy a battery can store, and how much solar energy you can realistically put back the next day.
 A solar generator can be one of those purchases that feels completely unnecessary right up until the first blackout, long camping trip, RV stop without hookups, or workday when the power disappears.
 It can also become an expensive box sitting in a closet if you buy one without a clear job for it.
 So instead of asking whether solar generators are universally "good," this guide answers the more useful question: is getting one worth the money for the way you actually live?

 Potentially very worthwhile 
 Solar can replace part or all of the energy used each day when the system is correctly sized 
 Hybrid solar plus fuel backup if daily loads exceed realistic solar recovery 
 The simplest rule: a solar generator becomes more valuable when you have a repeatable need, manageable loads, and a reliable recharge plan. It becomes less valuable when your expectations are larger than the battery and solar array.
 What Are You Actually Buying When You Buy a Solar Generator?
 Despite the name, a portable solar generator is not an engine that continuously generates electricity.
 For the type of product most shoppers are considering, it is better understood as two parts:
 Portable power station: battery, inverter, charging electronics, battery-management system and output ports.
 Solar panel: converts sunlight into DC electricity that can recharge the power station.
 Solar panel → portable power station → your devices 
 The battery is what keeps your devices running at night, indoors or when clouds pass overhead. Solar is one of the ways you refill that battery.
 This distinction matters because two products advertised as "1,200W solar generators" can have completely different battery capacities. Likewise, two products with similar battery capacity can accept very different amounts of solar input.
 If you want a deeper explanation of the charging process, see Can You Charge a Portable Power Station With a Solar Panel? 
 The Solar Generator Worth-It Score
 Use this before you look at brands or sale prices. Give yourself the points shown for each answer.
 1. How often do you expect to use it? Never or almost never: 0 points
Once or twice a year: 1 point
Several times a year or for one high-consequence backup need: 2 points
 2. Do you have a clearly defined load? "I want to power everything": 0 points
I know some of the devices: 1 point
I know the devices, watts and desired runtime: 2 points
 3. Do quiet operation and indoor battery use matter? Not at all: 0 points
Somewhat: 1 point
Very important: 2 points
 4. Do you have useful solar access? Mostly shade or no place to deploy panels: 0 points
Occasional usable sunlight: 1 point
Reliable open-sky access during camping, RV use or outages: 2 points
 5. Do you have another way to recharge? No realistic recharge method: 0 points
One method only: 1 point
Wall plus vehicle and/or solar options: 2 points
 Total Score 
 What It Means 
 Recommended Next Step 
 8–10 
 A solar generator is likely to deliver real value for you 
 Calculate battery capacity and panel size before choosing a model 
 5–7 
 It may be worth it, but the setup matters 
 Pay particular attention to battery capacity, daily energy use and recharge conditions 
 0–4 
 You may be paying for capacity or solar capability you rarely use 
 Compare a power bank, conventional UPS, gas generator or other backup option first 
 This score is a practical buying framework, not an industry certification.
 What Makes a Solar Generator Worth the Money?
 1. One Device Can Solve Several Problems
 A good portable solar generator does not have to earn its value from one blackout.
 The same unit can move between:
 Home outage backup
 RV travel
 Camping
 Tailgating
 Remote work
 Photography and drone charging
 Outdoor projects
 Emergency communications
 That multi-use value is important. A $1,000 piece of equipment used only once is a very different purchase from the same equipment used on ten camping weekends, several outages and regular outdoor projects.
 2. Quiet Indoor Battery Power Is Genuinely Useful
 A battery power station does not burn gasoline while supplying your devices. That makes it fundamentally different from a portable combustion generator.
 The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission states that portable fuel generators should be operated outdoors only, at least 20 feet away from a home, with exhaust directed away from the building.
 See CPSC carbon monoxide and portable-generator safety guidance .
 For an apartment, bedroom, RV or late-night campsite, being able to run a battery-based power station without a combustion engine is a meaningful benefit rather than a minor feature.
 3. Solar Gives the Battery a Recovery Path
 A battery without a recharge source eventually reaches zero. Solar changes the problem from "How long will the battery last?" to "Can I replace enough of what I use each day?"
 That is one of the biggest differences between short-term battery backup and a useful off-grid energy system.
 4. Low-Watt Essentials Stretch a Battery Surprisingly Far
 Phones, routers, LED lights, laptops, fans and similar loads use a fraction of the power demanded by space heaters, electric cooktops or large air conditioners.
 A well-planned essentials-only setup can therefore deliver much more useful backup time than a shopper might assume from battery capacity alone.
 5. You Avoid Routine Fuel-Engine Tasks
 Battery systems do not require gasoline storage, oil changes, spark plugs or pull-starting. You still need to store and maintain the battery according to the manufacturer's instructions, keep it charged, and test your emergency setup periodically, but routine ownership is generally simpler.
 When Is a Solar Generator Not Worth Getting?
 You Want the Lowest Upfront Cost for High Continuous Power
 A fuel generator can deliver substantial continuous power for its purchase price and can be refueled quickly. If your main requirement is running large loads for extended periods and you have a safe outdoor operating location plus dependable fuel access, a battery system may not be the cheapest answer.
 Your Main Load Is Electric Heat
 High-output heaters, electric kettles, hair dryers, hot plates and similar resistance loads turn battery capacity into heat very quickly.
 Even if the inverter can operate the appliance, that does not mean doing so for hours is practical.
 You Expect Normal Whole-House Living During a Blackout
 A portable solar generator is typically an essentials-first tool. Running central air conditioning, electric water heating, dryers, ranges and every household circuit as if grid power were still available requires a very different scale of energy storage and electrical integration.
 For a more detailed explanation, read Can a Solar Generator Power a House? 
 You Have No Useful Place to Put Solar Panels
 If your yard is heavily shaded or your apartment has no practical outdoor solar exposure, the solar portion of the purchase may provide limited value.
 You can still use the power station and recharge from the wall or a vehicle, but you should not pay extra for a large solar array you cannot effectively deploy.
 You Only Need a Few Phone Charges
 If all you want is to keep one or two phones alive during a rare outage, a smaller USB power bank is cheaper, lighter and easier to store.

Watts = how much power you can use at one moment.

 The Solar Recovery Test Most Buyers Skip
 Runtime tells you how fast the battery empties. For multi-day use, the more important question is how much energy you can put back.

 Example B: 1,200Wh Used, 735Wh Recovered

 Example C: 600Wh Used, 1,000Wh Recovered

 A solar generator becomes especially worthwhile when your daily solar recovery is reasonably close to your daily energy consumption. That is a better measure of off-grid usefulness than battery capacity alone.
 Is a Solar Generator Financially Worth It?
 If your only goal is lowering a normal residential electricity bill, a portable solar generator is generally the wrong product to evaluate as an investment.

 What Should You Check Before Buying a Solar Generator?
 Step 1: List the Devices You Actually Need
 Do not start with every appliance in your house. Start with the things you would genuinely miss during an outage or off-grid trip.
 Step 2: Add the Watts of Devices Running at the Same Time
 This determines the continuous AC-output requirement. Appliances with motors or compressors may also have higher startup requirements.
 Step 3: Calculate Watt-Hours
 Multiply each device's average power by the number of hours you expect to use it. This tells you how much battery capacity you actually need.
 Step 4: Decide How Much Energy You Want to Recover Each Day
 If your daily load is 900Wh, a tiny panel that recovers only a few hundred watt-hours on a good day may extend runtime but will not make the system energy-neutral.
 Step 5: Check Solar Voltage, Current and Input Limits
 Do not judge compatibility by connector shape alone. The panel's voltage, current and array configuration must stay within the power station's published solar-input limits.
 Step 6: Think About Where the Panels Will Actually Go
 A foldable panel is useful because you can move and angle it, but only if you have access to direct outdoor sunlight. Trees, buildings, railings and partial shadows can change production significantly.
 Step 7: Check Weight Before Buying the Biggest Battery
 A larger battery provides longer runtime but is harder to move. If you camp frequently, lifting and storage may matter as much as raw capacity.
 Step 8: Test the Setup Before You Need It
 Run your real devices from the station at home. Measure how quickly the battery falls and how much solar input you see under your local conditions. A practice run is more useful than relying on an ideal specification.
 The best solar generator is not automatically the largest one. It is the smallest practical system that can safely handle your peak load, provide the runtime you actually need, and recover enough energy for the way you plan to use it.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is it really worth getting a solar generator?
 Yes, if you have a clear use for quiet portable power, such as home outages, camping, RV travel, CPAP backup, refrigeration, remote work or off-grid electronics. It is less worthwhile if you only need occasional phone charging or expect a portable unit to run an entire home for days.
 What is the biggest disadvantage of a solar generator?
 The biggest limitation is finite stored energy combined with variable solar recharging. When the battery is depleted, you must recharge it, and solar charging speed depends on sunlight, panel size, weather, temperature, shading and the power station's input limit.
 Is a solar generator worth it for power outages?
 It is often worth it for essentials-first outage planning. Phones, routers, lights, laptops, fans, CPAP equipment and planned refrigerator use are much easier to support than whole-home heating, central air conditioning or several high-watt appliances running continuously.
 Is a solar generator worth it if I already have a gas generator?
 It can be. The two systems solve different problems. A battery solar generator is convenient for quiet indoor essential loads, while a fuel generator is useful for longer high-power situations when it can be safely operated outdoors and fuel is available. Some households use both as layers of the same emergency plan.
 Can a solar generator power a refrigerator?
 Many appropriately sized solar generators can run refrigerators, but you must check both the refrigerator's startup requirement and its energy use over time. Runtime depends more on actual average energy consumption and compressor cycling than on the refrigerator's maximum watt rating alone.
 Can a solar generator power a whole house?
 A portable solar generator can power selected household essentials, but most portable systems are not designed to run an entire home exactly as if utility power were available. Whole-home HVAC, electric heating, dryers, ranges and 240V circuits require a different scale of backup system.
 How big of a solar generator do I need?
 Start with simultaneous running watts, then calculate watt-hours. The inverter must support the appliances you plan to use at the same time, while battery capacity must cover the number of hours you need them to run. After that, size the solar array according to how much energy you want to recover each day.
 Do solar generators work on cloudy days?
 Solar panels can still produce electricity under some cloudy conditions, but output can be much lower than under strong direct sunlight. Do not build an emergency plan around receiving the panel's rated wattage every day.
 Do I need solar panels when I first buy a portable power station?
 No. A portable power station can normally be charged from another supported source such as wall power, and many models also support vehicle charging. Solar panels become more valuable for camping, RV travel, multi-day outages and other situations where grid charging may not be available.
 How many solar panels should I buy?
 Choose panels according to your daily energy consumption and the power station's solar-input limits. More panel wattage can increase recovery speed only until you reach the station's supported voltage, current and power limits.
 Is a 1,000Wh solar generator enough?
 It can be enough for many essentials-first applications. At a 90% conversion-efficiency estimate, a 1,000Wh battery provides roughly 900Wh of usable AC energy. That could mathematically support a 100W average load for about nine hours, but actual runtime varies.
 How long will the UDPOWER S1200 last?
 Runtime depends on the load. Using its 1,190Wh capacity and a 90% planning efficiency, the mathematical estimate is about 21.4 hours at 50W, 10.7 hours at 100W, 5.4 hours at 200W and 2.1 hours at 500W.
 How long will the UDPOWER S2400 last?
 Using its 2,083Wh capacity and a 90% planning efficiency, the mathematical estimate is about 37.5 hours at 50W, 18.7 hours at 100W, 9.4 hours at 200W and 3.7 hours at 500W. Actual runtime depends on the connected devices and operating conditions.
 Are solar generators safe to use indoors?
 Battery-based portable power stations do not burn gasoline or produce carbon monoxide exhaust during normal battery operation. Follow the manufacturer's ventilation, moisture, temperature and electrical instructions. Fuel-powered generators are different and should never be operated indoors or in a garage.
 Will buying a solar generator save money on my electric bill?
 A portable solar generator is usually purchased for backup power, portability and off-grid convenience rather than as the most economical way to reduce a normal household electricity bill. If utility-bill savings are your primary goal, compare a properly designed rooftop or installed solar system instead.
 Sources and Calculation Method
 Product specifications in this guide were checked against current UDPOWER product pages on August 26, 2026. Runtime examples use a 90% conversion-efficiency planning assumption and should be treated as estimates rather than guaranteed operating times.

 If you have defined essential loads, want quiet portable backup, and have a realistic wall, vehicle or solar recharge plan, a solar generator can be a very practical purchase.
 Start with the devices you actually need. Calculate watts, runtime and daily watt-hours. Then choose enough battery capacity and solar recovery without paying for capacity you will never use.

 What “Worth It” Really Means
 The mistake many buyers make is comparing a portable solar generator to the wrong thing. A portable solar generator is not a gas engine. It is a portable power station paired with solar panels. The battery stores energy. The inverter turns that stored energy into usable AC power. The solar panel gives you a way to recharge during daylight.
 That makes it excellent for controlled essential loads, but weak for unlimited power. The real value is not just “how many watts it has.” The real value is whether it solves a specific problem better than the alternatives.
 The practical value test
 A portable solar generator is usually worth buying when it saves you from one of these problems: no indoor-safe power during an outage, no quiet campsite power, no easy way to keep communication devices charged, no backup for medical comfort devices such as CPAP, or no daylight recovery option during multi-day emergencies.

 When a Portable Solar Generator Is Not Worth It
 You want to run your whole house normally
 Central AC, electric water heaters, electric ovens, dryers, large well pumps, and whole-home heating are usually outside the realistic job description of a portable solar generator. For that, compare a standby generator, installed home battery, or professionally designed backup system.
 You plan to run heat-producing appliances for hours
 Space heaters, hot plates, hair dryers, kettles, and electric cookers often use 800W to 1,800W while running. A power station may be able to turn them on, but the battery will drain quickly. For emergency planning, use these devices briefly or choose lower-watt alternatives.
 You expect a small solar panel to refill a large battery fast
 A 120W or 210W portable panel is useful, but it does not produce rated output all day. Sun angle, cloud cover, heat, shading, and charge controller limits all affect output. Solar is best viewed as a daylight recovery tool, not a magic fast refill button.
 You only care about the lowest upfront cost
 Gas generators can deliver more raw power per dollar at purchase. Portable solar generators win on indoor-safe battery power, quiet operation, low maintenance, and everyday convenience—not on the cheapest possible high-watt backup.
 The 3-Part Worth-It Test
 Before comparing sale prices, answer these three questions. This prevents the most common regret purchase: buying enough output watts but not enough battery capacity, or buying a large battery with too little solar input.

 1. What do you need to power? 
 Output watts decide whether the device can run. 
 A 1,200W appliance needs a power station with enough continuous output and surge headroom.

 2. How long must it run? 
 Battery Wh decides how long the device can run. 
 A 60W laptop uses about 60Wh per hour before efficiency loss. 
 Use Wh, not just W, to size the battery. 
 3. How will you refill it? 
 Solar input and panel size decide whether multi-day use feels practical. 
 A large power station with one small panel may recover slowly in cloudy weather. 
 Match battery size with a realistic solar panel plan.

 Estimated runtime = battery capacity × 0.90 ÷ device running watts.

 FAQ
 Are portable solar generators actually worth the money? 
 Yes, if you need quiet, indoor-safe power for essentials, camping, RV use, CPAP backup, router backup, lights, phones, laptops, fans, or refrigerator support. They are less worth it if you expect whole-house power or long-running electric heat.
 Can a portable solar generator run a refrigerator? 
 Many larger portable solar generators can run a refrigerator, but runtime depends on the refrigerator’s average power draw, startup surge, room temperature, door openings, and battery capacity. For meaningful fridge backup, a 1,000Wh+ power station is usually more practical than a compact unit.
 How big of a portable solar generator do I need? 
 For phones, lights, and laptops, a compact unit may be enough. For CPAP, fan, router, and light emergency backup, a mid-size unit is better. For refrigerator support and longer outages, choose a larger unit such as a 1,000Wh to 2,000Wh-class power station.
 Do portable solar generators work on cloudy days? 
 Yes, but charging is slower. Clouds, shade, panel angle, and temperature can reduce solar input. A solar generator can still be useful on cloudy days, but you should not plan around full rated panel output.
 Are portable solar generators better than gas generators? 
 They are better for quiet operation, indoor battery use, low maintenance, and short-to-medium essential backup. Gas generators are usually better for high sustained loads, fast refueling, and long outages where fuel is available and outdoor operation is safe.
 Can I use a portable solar generator indoors? 
 You can use the battery power station indoors if the product is designed for indoor use because it does not burn fuel or produce exhaust. Do not use a gas generator indoors, in a garage, or in any enclosed space.
 Is solar charging enough for a multi-day outage? 
 It can help a lot, but it depends on your daily energy use, solar panel size, sunlight, and the power station’s solar input limit. Solar is most useful when you prioritize essentials and recharge during the best daylight hours.

 For many buyers, the UDPOWER S1200 offers the best balance of capacity, output, portability, and emergency usefulness. Choose the S2400 if you need longer runtime, higher output, and more backup headroom.

Quick Answer

Yes, a portable power station is worth buying if it solves a specific power problem that matters to you: keeping a refrigerator cold during an outage, running a CPAP overnight, keeping Wi-Fi and work equipment online, powering an RV or campsite, or providing electricity where a wall outlet is not available.

It is usually not worth buying if you only want to charge a phone, expect a portable battery to run central air conditioning or electric heat for days, or buy a large station without first calculating how much energy your equipment actually uses.

The best portable power station is not the biggest one you can afford. It is the smallest one that can safely handle your appliances, deliver the runtime you need, and be recharged before you need that energy again.

For most buyers, the real return on the purchase is not lower utility bills. It is avoiding disruption when power is unavailable.

A portable power station becomes most valuable when it protects specific essentials instead of trying to replace every circuit in the house.

Who Should Buy a Portable Power Station?

A portable power station makes the most sense when losing electricity creates a real inconvenience, expense, safety concern, or interruption to something you regularly do.

Situation	Worth Buying?	Why	Typical Capacity to Consider
Phones, tablets and small USB devices only	Usually no	A normal USB power bank is smaller and cheaper.	Power bank instead
Laptop, router, lights and small electronics	Often yes	You gain AC outlets, much more stored energy and longer backup time.	250–600Wh
CPAP overnight backup	Often yes	Power continuity can matter much more than the purchase price.	500–1,200Wh depending on settings and runtime
Refrigerator during outages	Often yes	It can help protect food during short and moderate outages when properly sized.	1,000–2,000Wh+
Weekend camping or RV use	Yes for frequent users	One battery can serve lighting, phones, laptops, fans, cameras, CPAP and compatible appliances.	500–2,000Wh
Central HVAC, electric heat or whole-home operation	Usually no for a single portable unit	These loads can require far more continuous power and stored energy.	Consider a larger home-energy system or generator strategy

If you are still learning what these products actually do, start with What Is a Portable Power Station? before comparing individual models.

The Four-Part Worth-It Test

Most buying guides start with battery size. That is too late. Before comparing watt-hours, use these four questions.

1. What happens if the power is unavailable?

If the answer is “my phone charges later,” a large power station probably has little value. If the answer is “the refrigerator warms up,” “I cannot use my CPAP,” “I lose a workday,” or “the camping trip becomes difficult,” backup power has a much clearer job.

2. Can a portable unit actually cover that job?

Check both watts and watt-hours. Watts determine whether the station can operate the load. Watt-hours determine how long it can continue doing so.

3. How will you replace the energy you use?

A 2,000Wh battery is useful for longer periods than a 500Wh battery, but both eventually become empty. For multi-day outages and off-grid use, charging speed can matter almost as much as battery capacity.

4. How often will the station solve the problem?

A station used for outages, RV weekends, camping, remote work and road trips can justify itself more easily than one purchased for a single hypothetical event and never tested again.

A useful way to think about value:
Worth = importance of the load × frequency of use × backup coverage ÷ total ownership cost

You do not need to calculate a precise dollar answer. The formula forces you to ask whether the battery protects something you genuinely care about.

What Makes a Portable Power Station Worth the Money?

Portable power stations generally do not make financial sense as a way to buy cheap electricity. Grid electricity is difficult for a portable battery to beat after you include the initial purchase price.

The economic value comes from what the stored electricity prevents or enables.

Value	What the Power Station Can Prevent or Enable	Why It Matters
Food protection	Refrigerator or freezer support during an outage	Stored energy can be more valuable than its normal utility cost when it protects a full refrigerator.
Work continuity	Router, modem, laptop, monitor and phone charging	One uninterrupted workday can matter more than the cost of the electricity consumed.
Sleep equipment	Compatible CPAP equipment	Overnight continuity can justify a dedicated backup solution.
Travel flexibility	Camping, RV, road-trip and mobile equipment	The same battery can be used outside emergencies.
Quiet indoor backup	Lights, communications and electronics	Battery operation does not require a gasoline engine running beside the home.
Emergency readiness	Phones, radios, lighting and selected essential loads	The energy is already stored and available when the grid goes down.
Cost per meaningful use is more useful than cost per kWh
Cost per meaningful use = total system cost ÷ number of times it solves a real problem

A “meaningful use” might be an outage, a night of CPAP backup, a full camping day, a remote work shift, a tailgate, a field project or an RV travel day.

This is a better way to judge the purchase than asking whether recharging from the grid saves money on your electric bill.

How Much Portable Power Station Capacity Do You Actually Need?

The most common way to waste money is to start shopping before creating a load list.

Write down every device you expect to run, its wattage and the number of hours it needs to operate.

Energy needed (Wh) = device watts × hours of operation

For AC loads, the full battery label capacity is not normally available at the outlet because the inverter and electronics consume some energy. For UDPOWER planning examples, this guide uses a 90% conversion-efficiency estimate.

Estimated battery capacity required = total AC energy needed ÷ 0.90
Example 1: Remote work during a short outage
Load	Planning Use	Energy
Laptop	60W × 5 hours	300Wh
Router	12W × 5 hours	60Wh
Phone	One day's charging	20Wh
LED light	10W × 3 hours	30Wh
Total		410Wh

After allowing for AC conversion loss and reserve, a roughly 600Wh-class station is a much more practical target than a 250Wh model.

Example 2: One CPAP night

A CPAP drawing an average of 40W for eight hours would use about 320Wh before additional loads or conversion losses. Heated humidifiers and heated tubing can materially increase consumption, so use your actual machine settings whenever possible.

For a dedicated calculation, see How Long Will a CPAP Run on a Battery Backup?.

Example 3: Refrigerator plus basic outage essentials
Load	Planning Example	Energy Over 12 Hours
Refrigerator	80W average while planning	960Wh
Router	12W	144Wh
LED lighting	30W for 5 hours	150Wh
Phones	Two phones	40Wh
Total load energy		1,294Wh
Planning battery capacity at 90%	1,294 ÷ 0.90	About 1,438Wh before additional reserve

A refrigerator does not normally draw one constant wattage. Compressor cycling, room temperature, door openings and startup demand all affect actual use. A plug-in watt meter measured over several hours is more useful than guessing from a generic refrigerator wattage chart.
